Empirical Research Plan  
“Increased School Spending, Educational Attainment, and Adult Earnings”

----------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
----------------------------------------------------
Primary:  Staggered Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study (Sun-Abraham / Callaway-Sant’Anna estimator).  
Why appropriate:  
• School-finance court rulings occur in different states at different times (1955-1985) → plausibly exogenous shocks to district funding.  
• We observe individuals before and after the shock and a comparison group that is never (or later) treated.  
• PSID gives individual outcomes many years after schooling → long-run effects can be traced.

Supplementary:  Two-stage least squares (2SLS) that instruments district per-pupil spending with the interaction of (i) a post-reform indicator and (ii) the district’s pre-reform spending gap relative to the state mean (“differential-exposure” design à la Jackson-Johnson-Persico).  
The IV converts reduced-form DID effects into marginal returns to dollars.

----------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
----------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
• Treat_it = 1 if student i attended K-12 in state s during or after the first year the court order increased the state’s funding formula (year_ruling_s).  
• Exposure window: define the grade in which the child is observed in year t. Baseline: a child is “treated” if at least half of his/her K-12 years fall post-reform.

Control (counterfactual)  
• Same-state cohorts attending school before the ruling, plus cohorts in states that have not yet reformed by the same calendar year (“not-yet-treated”).  
• We will drop states that reform after 1985 to avoid right-censoring.

Treatment timing / event date  
• Event time τ = school year – year_ruling_s. We will examine τ = –10 … +15.

----------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
----------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: In absence of reform, treated and control cohorts would have followed the same outcome trajectories.  
– Plausibility: Court rulings are triggered by legal challenges, not by contemporaneous changes in student ability or earnings; state-specific cohort trends can be flexibly controlled.

A2. No anticipatory behavioral change: Districts do not sharply raise spending before the decision is handed down.  
– Plausible because funding formulas are usually rewritten only after final verdicts.

A3. Exogeneity of exposure conditional on state and cohort FE.  
– Families do not sort precisely around the ruling year in anticipation (checked with pre-reform migration tests).

A4. Stable unit treatment value (no spillovers across states).  
– Reasonable; interstate spillovers in K-12 spending are minimal.

A5. No differential measurement error correlated with treatment.  
– We use audited Census of Governments spending series; courts do not alter reporting quality.

----------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Remedies
----------------------------------------------------
T1. Selective migration (families move to higher-funded districts after ruling).  
• Remedy: (i) restrict to “non-mover” PSID children (same state 5<->17); (ii) control for county-of-birth FE; (iii) test pre-trend in out-migration rates.

T2. Other state-level policy shocks (e.g., desegregation, Head Start, minimum wage laws).  
• Remedy: include state-by-year covariates for contemporaneous education reforms, state GDP, unemployment, unionization, and desegregation orders; add state-specific linear or quadratic trends.

T3. Heterogeneous treatment timing bias (two-way-FE contamination).  
• Remedy: abandon naïve TWFE; use event-study estimator that is robust to staggered timing (Sun & Abraham 2020) and stacked DID (C&S 2021).

----------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
----------------------------------------------------
```r
# -------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# -------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)          # fast high-dim FE
library(did)             # Callaway-Sant’Anna DID
library(sunab)           # Sun-Abraham convenience
library(ggplot2)

# -------------------------------------------------
# 1. Data load & merge
# -------------------------------------------------
psid  <- fread("psid_individual.csv")          # individual panel
spend <- fread("district_spending.csv")        # district-year

# Merge by district_id and year in which child is in grade g
psid[, grade_year := birth_year + grade]       # approximate
setkey(psid, district_id, grade_year)
setkey(spend, district_id, year)
dat <- spend[psid, nomatch = 0]

# -------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variables
# -------------------------------------------------
# Court reform year by state (pre-loaded table 'reform_year_state')
reform <- fread("state_reform_years.csv")
dat <- merge(dat, reform, by = "state")

dat[, treated := as.integer(grade_year >= reform_year)]
dat[, event_time := grade_year - reform_year]          # for event study

# Outcomes
dat[, yrs_school := educ_years]                        # completed schooling
dat[, l_earn      := log(adult_earnings)]

# Control set
controls <- c("race", "gender", "parent_edu", "parent_income_childage5",
              "state_gdp", "state_unemp")

# -------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main DID: Sun–Abraham via fixest
# -------------------------------------------------
feols_main <- feols(yrs_school ~ sunab(reform_year, grade_year) + 
                     parent_edu + parent_income_childage5 | state + birth_cohort,
                     cluster = ~state, data = dat)

etable(feols_main, se = "cluster")

# Adult earnings outcome
feols_earn <- feols(l_earn ~ sunab(reform_year, grade_year) + 
                     parent_edu + parent_income_childage5 | state + birth_cohort,
                    cluster = ~state, data = dat)

# -------------------------------------------------
# 4. IV version (only for cohorts 7–16 yrs old during exposure)
# -------------------------------------------------
dat[, post := (grade_year >= reform_year)]
dat[, pre_gap := (spend_pc_pre_reform_state - spend_pc_state_mean)]
dat[, IV := post * pre_gap]

iv_mod <- feols(l_earn ~ spend_pc | state + birth_cohort | IV ~ ., 
                cluster = ~state, data = dat)

# -------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: placebo leads (τ = –10 … –3)
# -------------------------------------------------
pretest <- coef(feols_main, agg = "leading")   # automatically available
print(pretest)

# or perform C&S DID as alternative
cs <- att_gt(yname = "yrs_school",
             tname = "grade_year",
             idname = "pid",
             gname = "reform_year",
             xformla = ~ race + gender + parent_edu,
             data = dat)
summary(cs)
ggdid(cs) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, lty = 2)
```

----------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
----------------------------------------------------
Economic theory (education as human-capital investment) suggests positive, concave returns. Prior empirical work implies:  
• A 10 percent increase in per-pupil spending during K-12 → +0.10 – 0.20 years of completed schooling (≈1–2 percentage-point increase in high-school graduation).  
• Earnings elasticity ≈ 1.0–1.5, so the same 10 percent spending shock may raise adult earnings by about 1–2 percent, larger for children from low-income families.

----------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0.5 = partially, 0 = doubtful)
----------------------------------------------------
C1. Parallel pre-trends visually and statistically verified…… 0.8  
C2. No anticipatory effects……………………………………… 0.9  
C3. No other simultaneous treatments biasing results……… 0.6  
C4. Stable composition / no selective attrition……………… 0.7  
C5. Appropriate estimator for staggered timing……………… 1.0  
Overall average…………………………………………………… 0.8

The design is likely credible but hinges on ruling out coincident state-level reforms and migration.
